newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain - US-Iraq, harvests hit hard.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain - US-Iraq, harvests hit hard.

text.p: Australian grains were rocked during the past week by the suspension of Iraq's oil-for-food promise by the United Nations and by the worst enemy of prices, the strengthening prospect of bumper world crops.
"It was a week of nothing but bad news for wheat," Phil Lindsay of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures Ltd said.
Cash and futures prices for wheat held up fairly well under the stream of bearish news, both falling about A$5.00 a tonne for Australian Standard White (ASW) over the week.

The week began with the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) confirming most analysts' views by forecasting a near-record 1996/97 Australian wheat crop of 18.8 million tonnes. This would form most of a 28.7 million tonne winter crop, near the 1983/84 record 29.96 million tonnes. But later in the week, private forecaster Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd put the wheat crop at 19.8 million tonnes, which would be second only to the record 1983/84 crop of 22 million tonnes if achieved.

The Australian Wheat Board (AWB), which traders believe has been consistently under-predicting the size of the crop, held its official forecast at 17.6 million tonnes during the week as it grappled with the effect of recent frost in Queensland.
The AWB will revise its crop forecast late on Monday.
Traders commented that with the U.S. wheat crop looking better than previously thought, grain markets were feeling heavy harvest pressure.
The markets feared the world would be awash with wheat at the Australian harvest peak in January/February, Lindsay said.

While the U.S. fired missiles at Iraq, Tuesday's suspension of the UN decision earlier this year to allow Iraq to sell US$2 billion worth of oil every six months to buy food and medicine was more adverse news for Australian wheat.

An agreement struck by the AWB earlier this year for Australia to sell 100,000 tonnes of wheat a month to Iraq had opened the prospect of that country reclaiming its position as one of Australia's biggest wheat buyers.

The suspension meant that there was little chance Australia could start shipments of old crop wheat to Iraq, the AWB said. "This comes as a crushing blow to Australian wheatgrowers," Ord's Lindsay said at the close of the week. There was no panic selling in futures, but it was another negative factor, he said.
Big-crop fears could begin to spark some life in Australia's cash and futures markets for wheat by tempting users to sell forward, traders said at the end of last week.
"I think (sellers) will have to come into the market sooner or later, we've had a lack of forward selling to date," Peter Howard of New England Agricultural Traders said.
Cameron Pratt of GrainCorp said cash prices of ASW fell about A$5 during the week to the low A$180s.
Sorghum ended about A$200 Sydney or A$195 Newcastle delivered October, down about A$5 for deferred months.
Buying interest had evaporated for feed barley, he said.
Howard saw cash wheat prices down by A$3-A$4 over the week with ASW's last trade at A$181 into Newcastle.
The AWB's indicative price for new crop ASW wheat delivered Newcastle fell by A$2 to A$179 over the week.
Australian wheat futures edged back during the week, with the most frequently-traded January contract's settlement price falling to A$183.50 on Friday from A$188.00 Monday.
A total of 54 futures contracts changed hands in the week, while 24 January call options traded, most of them at a A$200 strike price, with premiums ranging between A$4 and A$5.
